name: Windsor knot

lead: The Windsor knot is a broad, symmetrical-looking triangle tied in the necktie. Because it is large, it fills the space between the collar points of a spread or cutaway collar and gives the neckline a structured, formal finish.

It takes its name from Edward, Duke of Windsor, although the Duke reportedly did not invent it; his wide knots came from thick tie fabric. Style discussion, including on T Nation, treats it as a traditional business and formal choice, with some members preferring it and others calling it heavy.

paras: It is tied with the wide end of the tie started well below the narrow end and wrapped several times before tightening, so it uses more tie length than a four-in-hand or half-Windsor. Men pair it with spread collars and thinner tie fabrics, and use the half-Windsor when they want something smaller.
There are no health risks. Practical drawbacks people mention are the length of tie it consumes, a bulky look with thick fabrics or narrow collars, and, to some, an overly formal or dated impression.

angle.text: The knot changes how the neck and collar area read: it is wider and fuller than other common knots, so it frames the face with a more structured triangle of fabric. Men use it with suits and spread collars when they want a formal result.

lead: The Windsor knot, also called the full Windsor, is a necktie knot with a wide, roughly triangular shape. Its width makes it especially suited to spread or cutaway collars.[1][2]

It improves a man's look at the neckline by giving a fuller, more balanced knot that fills the collar opening, in contrast to the narrower four-in-hand. The tie hangs from a larger, more deliberate knot, which many style writers associate with formality.[1]

The name refers to Edward VIII, the Duke of Windsor. Reference sources suggest the Duke's signature wide knot came from thicker ties, with the Windsor method later devised to get a similar look from ordinary ties; the Duke himself reportedly denied inventing it.[1][2]

paras: The knot is a wide triangle with the wide end of the tie draping over the narrow end. It is wider than most common knots and more balanced than the four-in-hand, though not perfectly symmetric.[2] A Grokipedia description lists a sequence of about seven wraps and notes that it needs more tie length than slimmer knots.[1]

The knot appeared in the early 1930s and carries the name of the Duke of Windsor.[1] Accounts differ on credit: some say the Duke or his London shirtmaker devised it, while others note that his wide knots came from thick tie fabric and that he said the method was adopted in America later.[1][2] A half-Windsor variant was developed as a smaller alternative.[2]

sections.h: Use in looksmaxxing and men's style
paras: On T Nation, forum members discuss tie knots in advice threads about interviews, weddings and funerals. One poster recommends tying a full Windsor for a med school interview, calling it the traditional trapezoidal knot.[3] Another recommends a half-Windsor for a wedding while a reply says a half-Windsor looks childish to some viewers.[4] A joke list of 'retrosexual' traits says a man should know only the Windsor, and another poster remarks that the Windsor is 'for cads'.[5][6] The range shows the knot is treated both as a formal default and as a matter of taste.

lore.intro: Men's fashion threads treat the Windsor as a classic formal option, with disagreement about whether it looks polished or heavy.[3][4][6]

claims.claim: A full Windsor is the proper knot for interviews and formal events
The Windsor is too large or old-fashioned for some men

timeline.event: The knot emerges publicly and becomes associated with Edward, Duke of Windsor.[1]
